One nice everyday touch comes from the papyri, where a third-century AD document recommends eating roots of bugloss to keep your breath from smelling after garlic, and an inscription uses ῥίζα for a royal ancestral line.

prose.def: To cause something to take root and become firmly fixed, used figuratively of being solidly established or grounded.
prose.article: ῥιζόω comes from the noun for "root" (ῥίζα) and literally means to cause something to take root, then figuratively to fix firmly or establish. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in a spiritual sense — being "rooted" in love (Eph. 3:17) and in Christ (Col. 2:7). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the word was used in everyday Koine of founding cities and even building a bridge ("αἰώνιος ἐρρίζωται," rooted forever), which helps explain why Colossians can shift so smoothly from rooting to building imagery.
prose.caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (and none in the critical SBLGNT text), the measured range is thin and rests heavily on metaphorical usage.

prose.def: A split-second moment, as quick as the blink of an eye.
prose.article: ῥιπή names an extremely brief moment, the time it takes to blink—every one of its single New Testament uses (1 Corinthians 15:52) is rendered "instant," matching the famous KJV phrase "twinkling of an eye." The word comes from ῥίπτω ("to throw"), and in classical Greek it covered any rapid movement: a thrown javelin, a rush of wind or flame, the flapping of wings, the flicker of lights. Notably, some manuscripts (D*EFG and others) read the similar-looking ῥοπή instead, a word meaning the tipping or turn of a balance-scale, which everyday Koine papyri use for "a moment" or to tip the scales in someone's favor.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and several manuscripts substitute the similar word ῥοπή, so the textual reading is disputed.

prose.def: To fan or stir something up with air, especially to drive waves or leaves into motion by a breeze.
prose.article: ῥιπίζω comes from the word for a fan or bellows, and its root sense is to fan a fire or make a breeze. In its one New Testament appearance (James 1:6), it describes a person whose doubt makes them like a wave of the sea "blown and raised with the wind," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it in terms of "doubts" 100% of the time. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from the papyri and Aristeas 70, where ornamental metal leaves are crafted so lifelike that they stir when a breath of wind fans them — showing the word's gentle "stirred by shifting breezes" feel rather than violent storm imagery.

prose.def: To toss or fling something about, as with garments thrown into the air.
prose.article: This is a strengthened form of ῥίπτω ("to throw, cast, hurl"), appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 22:23, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "tossing" — and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100%. The interesting wrinkle is that lexicographers disagree about which shade of meaning fits that single verse: some read it as the crowd "throwing off" their garments (as the KJV's "cast off"), while others, like Abbott-Smith, take it as the related sense "to shake, toss, throw about." In the Septuagint the underlying verb chiefly translates the Hebrew shalak ("to cast").
prose.caution: This form occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources openly disagree on whether it means "throw off" or "toss about" in that lone verse.

prose.def: To throw, fling, or toss something or someone, often quickly or carelessly, including casting things away or down.
